title: Adaptive Phase Stitching with Deadline-Aware Hedging for Mixed-Latency Workloads
creator: Maya Patel
description:
Summary: This ticket prototypes and implements 'phase stitching' — an alternative to aggressive phase splitting — that merges compatible prefill and decode work for similar requests to reduce redundant attention/KV work and improve p50/p95 latency and overall throughput. The twist: combine stitching with a deadline-aware hedging controller that selectively triggers speculative decode hedges only when deadline headroom is insufficient and fairness constraints permit it.

Motivation: Many tail-latency wins we've seen from splitting phases come at a cost: increased context fragmentation, KV cache misses, and unfairness toward long-running requests. For prefix-heavy workloads (chatbots with repeated prompts), we can avoid duplicate prefill compute by detecting compatible prefixes and stitching their prefill phases, then steering decode scheduling with fine-grained deadline budgets. This is particularly important for Dedicated customers who pay for throughput but need predictable latency SLOs.

Goals:
- Reduce redundant prefill work for similar prefixes by at least 35% in synthetic chat traces.
- Improve aggregate p95 latency for mixed short/long requests by 10-15% without regressing throughput.
- Maintain per-customer fairness: no request should be demoted below 90% of baseline latency SLA because of stitching.
- Provide telemetry hooks for per-phase cache reuse, hedging events, and starvation alerts.

Design overview:
1) Compatible request detection: lightweight fingerprinting of prefix token hashes + generation constraints; match threshold tuned to avoid semantic mismatch.
2) Prefill stitching: when multiple compatible prefill requests are queued, run a single prefill and attach resulting KV snapshot to each consumer request; ensure copy-on-write semantics so downstream decode sees correct KV context.
3) Deadline-aware hedging controller: each request has a deadline budget derived from route SLO and user priority. If decode scheduling detects that expected decode completion exceeds deadline headroom, controller may spawn a speculative hedge on a different allocation. Hedging triggers are gated by fairness tokens and a global hedging cap.
4) Fairness budget: per-tenant and per-route fairness counters ensure that aggressive stitching or hedging by one tenant doesn't starve others. Budget is replenished proportionally to historical SLA compliance.
5) Kernel/attention interplay: stitching increases contiguous KV cache hits and lets kernel selection favor fused attention paths for long common prefixes. We add an annotated hint to kernel selector indicating 'stitch-friendly' KV locality so the compiler can prefer optimized kernels that exploit cache locality.

Trade-offs and mitigations:
- Semantic drift risk if compatible detection is too loose. Mitigation: start with conservative hash threshold and A/B test with failsafe that falls back to isolated prefill if logs show divergence in outputs.
- Memory pressure from holding multiple KV snapshots. Mitigation: use copy-on-write references and TTL-based eviction tied to request timeouts.
- Complexity in debugging: added telemetry, tracing links to PRs and synthetic replay tooling to reproduce stitching decisions.

Implementation plan (phases):
A) Prototype (2 sprints): implement lightweight prefix fingerprinting, in-memory stitch coordinator, and controller; add basic telemetry (stitch count, reuse rate). Run offline replay on historical traces.
B) Canary (1 sprint): deploy to 5% of traffic on a non-critical region; enable deadline hedging in passive monitoring mode (no actual hedges) to collect prediction accuracy.
C) Active canary (2 sprints): enable hedging with strict caps; collect p50/p95/p99, KV hit rate, cache pressure, and fairness counters.
D) Gradual rollout (1-2 sprints): expand to higher traffic while tuning thresholds, kernel hints, and hedging caps.

Metrics / success criteria:
- Prefill work reduction: percentage decrease in prefill FLOPs per request at p50/p95. Target 35% reduction for compatible groups.
- Latency: p95 reduction >=10% and no regression in p50/p99 beyond 5% relative to baseline.
- Hedging efficiency: hedges improve deadline success rate by at least 20% for hedged requests and less than 2% waste (hedged runs that were unnecessary).
- Fairness: 95th-percentile of per-tenant latency ratio (stitch-enabled vs baseline) < 1.1.

Operational concerns / observability:
- New traces: stitch.event, stitch.group_id, kv.snapshot_id, hedge.spawned, hedge.outcome, fairness.credit_delta.
- Alerts: spike in stitch-induced semantic divergence, memory pressure from retained snapshots, fairness credit exhaustion for any tenant.
- Playbook: revert knob that disables stitching globally, fall back to per-request isolation in config, and manually reduce hedging cap.

Rollout and testing:
- Unit tests: stitch coordinator correctness, copy-on-write semantics, deadlock-free snapshot lifecycle.
- Integration tests: end-to-end replay against production-like traces; compare outputs to ensure no semantic regressions.
- Load tests: measure kernel selector shifts under high KV locality and validate no CPU/GPU regressions.
- Customer trials: invite two Dedicated customers with prefix-heavy workloads for early feedback.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Best eviction TTL for snapshots to balance memory vs reuse? (Experiment candidate)
- How to integrate with model-variant fallbacks when a stitch-produced KV snapshot is incompatible with a forced variant change?
- Should we expose a per-route opt-out for customers that prefer strict isolation?

Links and artifacts:
- Design doc (internal): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Phase+Stitching+Design
- Replay harness PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4218
- Initial experiment dashboard: https://dash.redwood.ai/d/abc123/stitching-experiments

Next steps: finalize prototype API for KV snapshot handles, land the stitch coordinator in a feature branch, and schedule replay runs on last 30 days of chat traffic. Owners: Liam O'Connor (runtime lead), Maya Patel (schedule/experiments), Theo Ramirez (platform telemetry).
